transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-18
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Evan Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Michael Zhang (Astoria, Head of ML), Rosa Vega (Astoria CTO), Daniel Kim (Astoria Infra)

Summary:
Redwood ran through Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV cache strategies and a simple cost model tailored to Astoria's payments workloads. Discussed tradeoffs for latency-sensitive flows (fraud detection) vs high-throughput batch jobs (reconciliation). Agreed to run a pilot in Astoria's VPC and share cost spreadsheet + security docs.

Topics:
- current infra and throughput targets
- prefix caching and KV cache logic
- batching strategies and autoscaling impact
- cost model assumptions (tokens/sec, cache hit rates, GPU TCO)
- security/compliance and benchmark plan

Action items (also in metadata): Evan to send cost model, Priya to draft benchmark plan, Michael to confirm compliance contacts.

Transcript:
[00:00:03] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Evan from Redwood, and Priya's with me \u2014 Priya's our systems SE, she'll do most of the deep dive. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:12] Michael: Good, thanks. We're excited \u2014 we've been looking at the Optimize stuff, specifically around batching and cache, because our fraud scoring needs are growing.
[00:00:20] Rosa: Hi, yes, want to make sure this helps with latency for the real-time flows and cost for overnight jobs.
[00:00:28] Priya: Great. Quick agenda \u2014 we'll cover a brief refresher on what prefix/KV cache does, then walk through batching strategies, show a simple cost model with assumptions, and end with recommended config and next steps.
[00:00:42] Daniel: Sounds good. Our baseline: ~200 reqs/sec for scoring, p95 latency target 200ms, and a batch job that does ~2M tokens overnight.
[00:00:53] Priya: Perfect, that helps. Two threads to keep in mind \u2014 latency SLO for real-time (fraud), and throughput/cost for batch jobs. Optimize gives levers for both: caching (prefix and KV) and dynamic batching.
[00:01:10] Priya: First \u2014 prefix cache. This caches repeated prompt prefixes at the token/KV level so you don't re-run the whole prefix each request. For Astoria, if your scoring prompts share a long shared context \u2014 e.g., policy text + user history \u2014 prefix caching can cut compute by 40-70% depending on hit rate.
[00:01:28] Michael: Quick question \u2014 is the prefix cache stateful on the GPU or in external KV? We need to understand data residency for compliance.
[00:01:36] Priya: Good call. We have two modes: local KV (node-local in-memory, fastest but per-host) and external KV (customer-managed Redis or S3-backed cold store). For Private deployments we can plug customer KMS and audit logs; for hosted we'll keep LLs ephemeral and offer encryption at rest. If you want auditability, the external KV option in your VPC is recommended.
[00:01:58] Rosa: So for us, external KV in our VPC + KMS is preferred.
[00:02:03] Evan: We'll include that in the pilot plan, and Priya will include KMS integration notes.
[00:02:10] Priya: Moving to batching \u2014 we have two strategies: latency-aware micro-batching for real-time (batch windows 5-20ms) to keep p95 low, and large asynchronous batching for throughput jobs. The runtime's continuous batching will group requests by model and token-length to maximize GPU utilization.
[00:02:29] Daniel: What's the expected latency hit for micro-batching? We can't exceed 200ms p95.
[00:02:34] Priya: For typical 2k-context scoring with a small output our tests show micro-batch add ~10-30ms average, p95 up to ~50ms depending on load. Worst case if we batch too long, yes that could push you past 200ms, but we tune the window and fallback to single-request execution if SLOs are at risk.
[00:02:50] Michael: And cost \u2014 how much do we save with batching?
[00:02:53] Priya: It varies. The cost model we showed assumes GPU TCO, tokens/sec, and cache hit rates. For example, with a 60% prefix cache hit and micro-batching of 8, you could see 35-50% reduction in token compute costs vs naive per-request execution. For batch jobs with good batching you can reduce cost per token by 2\u20133x. We'll send the sheet with assumptions so you can tweak.
[00:03:17] Evan: I'll pause here \u2014 there's a link to the cost model in the deck we shared (not in the transcript, but we'll include the sheet). Priya, show the chart for prefix hit-rate vs cost.
[00:03:29] Priya: (screen) Okay, chart \u2014 X axis is prefix hit rate, Y is effective cost per 1k tokens. You can see diminishing returns after ~80% because most of the prefix cost is avoided earlier. Note: hit rates depend on how standardized your prompts are \u2014 the payments scoring prompts looked like good candidates in our pre-call survey.
[00:03:50] Rosa: We do canonicalize prompts in the scoring path, yes \u2014 that should help. Does the KV cache support TTL eviction policies?
[00:03:59] Priya: Yes TTL and LRU. Also warm-up strategies: proactively pre-populate the cache for the batch windows to avoid cold misses. Warm-up can be scheduled as part of deployment or triggered by traffic patterns.
[00:04:12] Daniel: How does this interact with quantization or reduced-precision models? Any gotchas?
[00:04:17] Priya: Not much; quantization affects runtime kernels but cache entries are just key/value activations \u2014 they remain compatible as long as model variants are compatible. The main gotcha is versioning: if you rollout a new model variant, we invalidate or maintain separate cache namespaces. We recommend namespace per model version to avoid silent corruption.
[00:04:34] Michael: That makes sense. What about fallback \u2014 if cache misses spike, does the system autoscale?
[00:04:40] Priya: Yes, we have smart routing + autoscaling. If miss-rate increases, throughput drops per GPU; the autoscaler can add GPUs but there's lag. So we recommend conservative SLOs and pre-warm or keep a small headroom. There's also an option for burst capacity in Dedicated deployments to absorb spikes.
[00:04:55] Evan: Let's walk through a toy calculation for your numbers. You said 200 reqs/sec, p95 200ms target, and 2M tokens overnight. Priya, run the simplified cost model.
[00:05:05] Priya: Sure. Assumptions: baseline GPU cost $X/hour (we'll replace with your TCO in the sheet), average tokens per real-time req 60, prefix length 120 tokens, cache hit 60%. For real-time, effective tokens processed = 200 * 60 * (1 - 0.6) + overhead for KV lookups. That reduces compute tokens by ~48%. For overnight 2M tokens if we achieve the same 60% hit and large batching, cost per token is roughly 0.4x baseline.
[00:05:36] Rosa: Can you add bandwidth/redis costs for external KV into the spreadsheet? That can be material at scale.
[00:05:42] Evan: Good point \u2014 network egress, redis ops, and storage for cache entries will be in the sheet. We'll include a separate line item for external KV.
[00:05:50] Michael: We're also concerned about audit logs and retention for compliance. How granular are the access logs for cache reads/writes?
[00:05:57] Priya: We log cache evictions, misses, and hits as aggregates by default; for Private deployments we can enable per-request audit logs and ship them to your SIEM. For hosted customers we provide aggregated metrics and optional long-term retention as an add-on. We'll attach the SOC2/ISO docs and an audit log options doc.
[00:06:15] Daniel: What's the recommended setup for pilot? We prefer VPC deployment.
[00:06:20] Evan: Recommend Redwood Private in your VPC for the pilot \u2014 that gives you KMS integration and control over KV. For speed we can do a hosted pilot first, but given compliance you probably want VPC from day one.
[00:06:31] Michael: VPC pilot is preferred. Timeline?
[00:06:34] Evan: We can get a pilot environment in ~2 weeks once contracts and infra access are in place. Priya will draft the benchmark plan including a 2-hour real-time stress run and an overnight throughput test.
[00:06:44] Priya: I'll include test datasets \u2014 anonymized logs, typical prompt distribution, and a synthetic spike test for 5x baseline. We'll also capture token-level traces to validate KV hit rates.
[00:06:57] Rosa: On security, we'll need SSO/SAML and SCIM for user provisioning. Is that supported?
[00:07:03] Evan: Yes SSO + SCIM supported for Private and Dedicated. We'll include setup steps and an owner-level checklist.
[00:07:10] Michael: A couple of other things \u2014 how do rollouts work? If we can canary a new model or quantized variant without losing caches.
[00:07:17] Priya: Canary and A/B supported. Again namespace caches per model version. We also support automatic fallback\u2014if the canary misses the quality threshold, traffic can roll back to the baseline. We'll show the rollout UI in the Console in the follow-up demo.
[00:07:31] Daniel: Any concerns about shared GPU environments causing noisy neighbors?
[00:07:36] Priya: Dedicated pools avoid noisy neighbors. In Hosted we mitigate with QoS and routing, but for strict isolation Dedicated is the path. For your pilot in VPC Private we'll provision dedicated GPU nodes per your commit.
[00:07:49] Evan: Quick detour \u2014 competitors. Michael, curious if you evaluated Anthropic or OpenAI?
[00:07:55] Michael: Yep, we've POC'd both. Main differences for us are control (we need VPC/KMS) and predictable cost. Some vendors had lower latency in hosted, but lacked private deployment options.
[00:08:06] Evan: That's consistent with others. Our play is production controls + cost levers.
[00:08:10] Priya: Back to config recommendations for Astoria: 1) Enable external KV in your VPC, 2) TTL 24 hours + LRU and pre-warm for business hours, 3) Micro-batching window 10ms for real-time with single-request fallback, 4) Large batching for overnight jobs with batch sizes tuned by tokens-per-request, 5) Namespace cache by model version and include warm-up jobs during rollouts.
[00:08:33] Rosa: That sounds sensible. Any quick numbers for expected savings?
[00:08:37] Priya: With conservative assumptions we'll show 30\u201345% savings on the real-time path and 2x cost reduction for batch jobs. Exact numbers in the spreadsheet; we'll let you plug your TCO to get a tailored estimate.
[00:08:48] Michael: Ok. On the benchmarking instrumentation \u2014 what telemetry will we need? We want token-level cost, cache hit/miss, per-route latency.
[00:08:56] Priya: Console exposes per-route token counts, cache hit/miss, and latency histograms. For pilot we'll enable increased retention and raw traces for the 2-hour run. We'll also provide a lightweight tracing hook to correlate requests with your logs.
[00:09:10] Daniel: Any prerequisites from our infra team?
[00:09:13] Evan: Access to the VPC, a Redis cluster (or we'll propose managed Redis), KMS credentials for keywrap, and a service account for the benchmark agent. We'll include a checklist.
[00:09:23] Michael: Great. Let's talk next steps and owners.
[00:09:26] Evan: Action items \u2014 Evan: send cost model and pricing tiers by Friday 2027-05-20; Priya: benchmark plan + test dataset by 2027-05-25; Michael: confirm compliance contact and VPC access window by 2027-05-21. We'll schedule a 30-min kickoff for the pilot once access is confirmed.
[00:09:45] Rosa: One last Q \u2014 is there an SLA for latency under Dedicated / Private?
[00:09:50] Evan: Yes Dedicated has SLA-backed latency and uptime tiers. Private has contractual SLAs depending on the support tier. We'll include SLA options in the pricing doc.
[00:09:59] Michael: Awesome.
[00:10:01] Evan: Okay we'll follow up with the sheet and security docs. Thanks everyone.
[00:10:07] Rosa: Thanks, bye.
[00:10:09] Michael: Thanks.
